title: Work, Energy and Power
tagline: Relate work, energy forms, power and conservation in physical systems.

sourceNote.thirdParty: ICSE Class 10 Physics syllabus scope for the named chapter (inferred from standard board-prescribed topic titles); CISCE primary document not directly fetched in this environment. Content independently authored for Target95 BoardPrep.

overview.intro: Work, energy and power describe how forces cause motion and how energy is transferred or transformed. Work is done when a force produces displacement in its direction, energy is the capacity to do work, and power measures the rate of doing work. This chapter develops calculations involving work, kinetic and potential energy, conservation of energy, and power, with attention to units and practical interpretations.

learningOutcomes: Define work and calculate it for different directions of force and displacement.
Distinguish kinetic and potential energy and compute their values.
Apply work-energy relationships and conservation of mechanical energy.
Define power and efficiency and solve related numerical problems.
Use correct SI units and interpret positive, negative and zero work.

blocks.text: In physics, work is said to be done when a force acts on a body and produces displacement in the direction of the force or its component. The magnitude of work is given by W = F s cosθ, where θ is the angle between force and displacement. The SI unit of work is joule (J), equal to one newton metre.

Work can be positive, negative or zero. It is positive when force has a component in the direction of displacement, negative when it acts opposite to displacement (e.g. friction), and zero when there is no displacement or when force is perpendicular to displacement, such as centripetal force in uniform circular motion.

items.text: A 50 N force moves a box 4 m in the same direction: W = 50 × 4 = 200 J.
items.note: cos 0° = 1 when force and displacement are parallel.

items.text: Carrying a load horizontally at constant height: work done by upward force on load is zero.
items.note: Force is perpendicular to horizontal displacement.

blocks.text: Energy is the capacity to do work, and its SI unit is joule. Mechanical energy commonly appears as kinetic energy and potential energy. Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion and is given by KE = 1/2 mv^2, where m is mass and v is speed.

Potential energy is energy possessed by a body due to its position or configuration. Gravitational potential energy near Earth’s surface is PE = mgh, where h is height above a chosen reference level. Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed springs and other elastic bodies.

items: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed, so doubling speed quadruples KE.
Potential energy is relative to a reference level.
Work done against gravity increases gravitational potential energy.
Energy can change form but is measured in the same unit, joule.

blocks.text: Work done on a body can change its energy. The work-energy principle states that the net work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy. When a force speeds up a body, positive work increases kinetic energy; when it slows the body, negative work decreases kinetic energy.

The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only transformed from one form to another. In an ideal system with no non-conservative losses, total mechanical energy (KE + PE) remains constant. In real systems, some mechanical energy may transform into heat or sound due to friction.

Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, given by P = W/t. The SI unit of power is watt (W), where 1 W = 1 J/s. For a body moving at constant velocity under force F in the direction of motion, power can also be expressed as P = Fv.

Larger units include kilowatt (kW) and horsepower (hp) in some contexts, but SI calculations should use watts. Electrical energy consumption is often measured in kilowatt-hour (kWh), which is a unit of energy, not power: 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10^6 J. Efficiency compares useful output to total input, usually as a percentage.

items.meaning: Rate of doing work or transferring energy.
SI unit of power equal to one joule per second.
Commercial unit of electrical energy equal to energy used by 1 kW in 1 hour.

blocks.text: When solving problems, identify known quantities, convert units to SI where needed, and choose the appropriate relation (work, KE, PE, power). For vertical motion problems near Earth, use g as given or 9.8 m/s^2/10 m/s^2 as specified. Keep track of reference levels for potential energy.

In conservation of mechanical energy problems without losses, equate total energy at two positions: mgh1 + 1/2 mv1^2 = mgh2 + 1/2 mv2^2. If friction or other losses are present, account for energy dissipated. Clearly state assumptions such as neglecting air resistance when applicable.

items: Check angle between force and displacement before using W = Fs cosθ.
Use consistent units (kg, m, s, N, J, W).
State whether energy losses are neglected in conservation problems.

keyPoints: Work is done only when a force causes displacement, W = F s cosθ.
Work may be positive, negative or zero depending on direction relative to displacement.
Kinetic energy is 1/2 mv^2 and depends strongly on speed.
Gravitational potential energy near Earth is mgh relative to a chosen level.
Net work done on a body equals change in kinetic energy.
Total energy is conserved; mechanical energy is conserved only without losses.
Power is the rate of doing work, P = W/t, measured in watts.
Kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power.
Efficiency relates useful output energy/work to total input.
Correct units and angle/reference choices are essential in calculations.
examFocus: Calculate work for forces parallel, opposite or at an angle to displacement.
Solve numerical problems on KE, PE and conservation of mechanical energy.
Explain when work done is zero with examples.
Differentiate power and energy, and convert kWh to joules.
Apply P = W/t and P = Fv in appropriate contexts.
State and use the law of conservation of energy with transformations.
Show steps, units and assumptions in numerical answers.

questions.prompt: The SI unit of power is:
questions.explanation: Power is rate of doing work and its SI unit is watt (J/s).
questions.commonMistake: Kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not power.

questions.prompt: Kinetic energy of a body of mass m moving with speed v is:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on mass and the square of speed.
questions.commonMistake: mgh is gravitational potential energy.

questions.prompt: Work done is zero when the angle between force and displacement is:
questions.explanation: W = F s cosθ and cos 90° = 0, so no work is done.
questions.commonMistake: At 180° work is negative, not zero.

questions.prompt: If the speed of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is proportional to v^2, so (2v)^2 = 4v^2.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse linear dependence with square dependence.

questions.prompt: 1 kilowatt-hour is equal to:
questions.commonMistake: Convert both kilowatts to watts and hours to seconds.

questions.prompt: Gravitational potential energy of a mass m at height h is:
questions.explanation: Near Earth’s surface, potential energy increases linearly with height: PE = mgh.
questions.commonMistake: Ensure h is measured from the chosen reference level.

questions.prompt: A force doing negative work on a body generally:
questions.explanation: Negative work removes energy from the body, often reducing its speed and kinetic energy.
questions.commonMistake: Friction is a common example of a force doing negative work.

questions.prompt: A machine does 600 J of useful work when 800 J of energy is supplied. Its efficiency is:
questions.explanation: Efficiency = (useful output/input) × 100% = (600/800) × 100% = 75%.
questions.commonMistake: Efficiency cannot exceed 100% for a real machine.

questions.prompt: The capacity to do work is called ________.
questions.explanation: Energy is measured in joules, the same unit as work.
questions.commonMistake: Power is the rate of doing work, not the capacity.

questions.prompt: The power of a machine that does 1200 J of work in 4 s is ________ W.
questions.explanation: Power is work done divided by time taken: 1200 J ÷ 4 s = 300 W.
questions.commonMistake: Dividing time by work; power is work divided by time.

questions.prompt: According to the work-energy principle, net work done equals change in ________ energy.
questions.explanation: Net work changes the kinetic energy of the body.
questions.commonMistake: State kinetic energy specifically for the work-energy principle.

questions.prompt: Define work in physics and give its SI unit.
questions.answer: Work is done when a force produces displacement in the direction of the force or its component. It is given by W = F s cosθ and its SI unit is joule (J).
questions.explanation: Both force and displacement in the relevant direction are required for work.
questions.commonMistake: Everyday effort without displacement is not work in physics.

questions.prompt: State two situations in which work done by a force is zero.
questions.answer: Work done is zero when there is no displacement of the body despite a force acting, and when the force is perpendicular to the displacement (for example, centripetal force in uniform circular motion).
questions.explanation: In both cases, the force does not produce displacement in its direction.
questions.commonMistake: Give physically correct examples for each situation.

questions.prompt: Calculate the work done when a force of 40 N moves an object 5 m in the direction of the force.
questions.answer: Work done W = F × s (since force and displacement are in the same direction, cos 0° = 1). Therefore W = 40 × 5 = 200 J.
questions.explanation: Use the component of displacement along the force direction.
questions.commonMistake: Include the unit joule in the final answer.

questions.prompt: A body of mass 2 kg is moving at 3 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: Square the speed before multiplying by mass and 1/2.
questions.commonMistake: Do not forget to square the velocity term.

questions.prompt: Explain the law of conservation of energy with the example of a freely falling body (neglecting air resistance).
questions.answer: The law of conservation of energy states that energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only change from one form to another. For a freely falling body, at the highest point it has maximum gravitational potential energy and zero kinetic energy (if released from rest). As it falls, potential energy decreases while kinetic energy increases. Just before reaching the ground, potential energy is minimum and kinetic energy is maximum. Neglecting air resistance, the total mechanical energy (PE + KE) remains constant throughout the fall.
questions.explanation: Loss in potential energy equals gain in kinetic energy in an ideal case.
questions.commonMistake: State the assumption that air resistance is neglected.

questions.prompt: Differentiate between work, energy and power, giving SI unit of each.
questions.answer: Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction and is measured in joules (J). Energy is the capacity to do work and is also measured in joules (J). Power is the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, given by P = W/t, and is measured in watts (W). Thus, work and energy represent quantities, while power represents how fast that quantity is used or transferred.
questions.explanation: Units help distinguish related but different physical quantities.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse kilowatt-hour (energy) with kilowatt (power).

questions.prompt: A 5 kg object is raised vertically through a height of 10 m. Calculate the gain in potential energy. If this is done in 4 s, calculate the power developed. (Take g = 10 m/s^2.)
questions.answer: Gain in gravitational potential energy = mgh = 5 × 10 × 10 = 500 J. Power developed = work done/time = 500/4 = 125 W. Therefore, the gain in potential energy is 500 J and the power developed is 125 W.
questions.explanation: Raising the object at constant speed requires work equal to the increase in potential energy.
questions.commonMistake: Use the given value of g and include correct units for both answers.

questions.prompt: Two motors lift identical loads to the same height, but motor A takes 20 s while motor B takes 10 s. Compare the work done and power of the two motors.
questions.answer: Since the loads and heights are identical, the work done against gravity (mgh) is the same for both motors. Power is work done per unit time, so motor B develops twice the power of motor A because it does the same work in half the time (P = W/t).
questions.explanation: Equal work in less time means greater power.
questions.commonMistake: Do not assume different work when load and height are the same.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upwards. Describe the energy changes during its upward and downward motion, ignoring air resistance.
questions.answer: As the ball rises, its kinetic energy decreases while its gravitational potential energy increases because speed reduces with height. At the highest point, kinetic energy is momentarily zero (if thrown vertically) and potential energy is maximum. During downward motion, potential energy decreases and kinetic energy increases as speed increases. Ignoring air resistance, total mechanical energy remains constant throughout.
questions.explanation: Energy continuously transforms between kinetic and potential forms.
questions.commonMistake: Total mechanical energy stays constant only when losses are neglected.

questions.prompt: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s brakes to rest. Calculate its initial kinetic energy. If braking distance is 50 m, find the average braking force (assuming constant force and neglecting other losses).
questions.answer: Initial kinetic energy = 1/2 mv^2 = 1/2 × 1000 × (20)^2 = 500 × 400 = 200000 J. The work done by the braking force brings the car to rest, so work done = loss in kinetic energy = 200000 J. If F is the average braking force opposite to motion over 50 m, F × 50 = 200000, giving F = 4000 N. The average braking force is 4000 N opposite to the direction of motion.
questions.explanation: Work-energy principle links stopping force and distance to initial kinetic energy.
questions.commonMistake: Include the direction (opposing motion) and use consistent SI units.

questions.prompt: Explain why holding a heavy suitcase stationary does no work on the suitcase in the scientific sense, even though it feels tiring.
questions.answer: In physics, work requires displacement in the direction of the applied force. When the suitcase is held stationary, its displacement is zero, so the work done on the suitcase is W = F × 0 = 0. It feels tiring because muscles expend chemical energy internally to maintain tension and posture, but this internal physiological effort is not work done on the suitcase.
questions.explanation: Scientific work depends on displacement of the object acted upon.
questions.commonMistake: Distinguish physical sensation from the physics definition of work.
